overview.intro: The Modern Age in Europe begins with three revolutions of the mind and machine: the Renaissance (a rebirth of art, letters and science), the Reformation (a challenge to the Catholic Church that split Western Christendom), and the Industrial Revolution (the transformation of production by machine and factory). This chapter covers each in turn - definitions, causes, key personalities, impacts and consequences.

blocks.text: After the Crusades and the growth of towns, Europe's merchants and bankers - above all in Italy's city-states - had wealth and curiosity to spare. The fall of Constantinople (1453) sent Greek scholars west with classical manuscripts; the printing press multiplied books; maritime discoveries widened horizons. Into this world came the Renaissance (14th-16th c.), then the Reformation (16th c.), and - fed by colonial trade, capital and inventions - the Industrial Revolution (c. 1750-1850), which together created the modern world of science, nation-states, factories and new ideologies.

Renaissance - definition and causes. The Renaissance ('rebirth') was the revival of classical Greek and Roman learning and a new human-centred view of life, beginning in 14th-century Italy (Dante, Petrarch), flowering in the 15th-16th centuries. Causes: (1) the capture of Constantinople by the Ottoman Turks (1453) drove Greek scholars and manuscripts to Italy; (2) the decline of feudalism freed towns and individuals from feudal bonds; (3) new trade routes and the wealth of Italian city-states (Venice, Florence, Genoa) - and later Atlantic trade - financed culture; (4) the spirit of enquiry encouraged by contact with new lands and ideas; (5) Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1440-50) spread books and ideas cheaply and quickly.

Renaissance - impact on art, literature, science. Art: perspective, anatomy, realism and oil painting - Leonardo da Vinci (Mona Lisa, The Last Supper; notebooks of invention), Michelangelo (Sistine Chapel ceiling, David), Raphael (Madonnas, School of Athens). Literature: Petrarch's humanist sonnets, Erasmus's Praise of Folly, Cervantes' Don Quixote and, above all, William Shakespeare (1564-1616) - whose plays (Hamlet, Macbeth, King Lear, Romeo and Juliet) probed human nature with unmatched depth and enriched English forever. Science: observation and experiment replaced authority - Copernicus (De Revolutionibus, 1543) placed the sun at the centre of the universe (heliocentrism), later confirmed by Galileo's telescope and Kepler's laws; Vesalius founded modern anatomy; medicine and geography advanced.

Consequences of the Renaissance. It replaced other-worldliness with confidence in human ability; it encouraged voyages of discovery (Columbus, Vasco da Gama); it spread literacy and questioning through the press; it freed science from dogma; it created a vernacular literature (Italian, French, English); and it prepared the Reformation by teaching men to read and judge for themselves. In art and thought it set the standards of the modern West - individualism, realism and reason.

Reformation - meaning and causes. The Reformation was the 16th-century religious upheaval that broke the unity of Western Christendom and founded Protestant churches. Causes: dissatisfaction with the practices of the Catholic Church - the sale of indulgences, simony (buying offices), nepotism, immorality among clergy, and the lavish cost of St Peter's; the 'new learning' of the Renaissance taught men to read the Bible themselves (Erasmus's Greek New Testament) and to judge; national rulers resented papal taxes and interference; the printing press spread criticism far and wide.

Reformation - Martin Luther and the Counter Reformation. Martin Luther, a German Augustinian monk, protested against Tetzel's sale of indulgences by nailing his Ninety-Five Theses to the Wittenberg church door (31 October 1517). He taught salvation by faith alone (justification by faith), the Bible as the sole authority (scripture over pope), and the priesthood of all believers; excommunicated in 1521 (Diet of Worms), he translated the Bible into German and led a reformation that spread across northern Europe - aided by princes who seized church lands. Calvin (Geneva, predestination, discipline) and Zwingli extended it; in England, Henry VIII's break with Rome created the Anglican Church. The Counter Reformation answered: the Council of Trent (1545-63) reformed abuses and reaffirmed doctrine; the Jesuits (Ignatius Loyola) led education and missions; the Inquisition enforced orthodoxy; and the Church recovered much of southern Europe.

Industrial Revolution - definition and causes. The Industrial Revolution was the change from hand production at home to machine production in factories - from human/animal power to steam - beginning in Britain c. 1750-1850 and spreading worldwide. Causes: (1) colonial and maritime trade accumulating capital and providing raw materials (cotton) and markets; (2) coal and iron ore in Britain, plus canals and roads; (3) agricultural revolution (enclosures, crop rotation) freeing labour and feeding cities; (4) a chain of inventions - Kay's flying shuttle (1733), Hargreaves's spinning jenny (1764), Arkwright's water frame, Crompton's mule, Cartwright's power loom, Watt's improved steam engine (1769), and later locomotives (Stephenson) and steamships; (5) political stability, patent laws and laissez-faire policy encouraging enterprise; (6) abundant capital from trade and banking, and a labour supply from enclosure.

Capitalism - meaning and rise. Capitalism is an economic system in which private persons own the means of production (factories, machines, capital) and produce for profit in a competitive market, with wages paid to workers who own no capital. Causes of its rise: profits of colonial trade and banking; the price revolution (American silver) rewarding enterprise; the dissolution of feudal restraints; enclosures creating free labour; inventions making factory investment profitable; and governments' laissez-faire policies protecting property and contracts. Capitalism financed the Industrial Revolution and was intensified by it - factories, joint-stock companies, stock exchanges and a wage-earning class.

Socialism - meaning and rise. Socialism is the doctrine that the means of production should be owned or controlled by society (the state or the community) so that wealth serves all, ending the exploitation of labour by capital. Causes of its rise: the miseries of industrial workers - long hours, child and female labour, urban slums, unemployment and the cyclical misery of glut and slump; the glaring inequality of capitalist wealth; and the ideas of thinkers - Saint-Simon, Charles Fourier and Robert Owen (experiments and reform), then Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (the Communist Manifesto, 1848; Das Kapital, 1867), who taught class struggle and called workers to unite. Trade unions, Chartism, factory acts and, eventually, socialist parties and revolutions (Russia, 1917) flowed from this tradition.

items: Leonardo da Vinci - Painter of Mona Lisa and The Last Supper; anatomist, engineer - the 'Renaissance man'.
William Shakespeare - England's greatest dramatist (1564-1616): Hamlet, Macbeth, King Lear - human nature on stage.
Nicolaus Copernicus - Astronomer whose De Revolutionibus (1543) set the sun, not the earth, at the centre.
Johannes Gutenberg - Invented movable-type printing press (c. 1440-50).
Martin Luther - German monk; Ninety-Five Theses (1517); salvation by faith; Bible in German.
John Calvin - Geneva's reformer: predestination and strict church discipline.
Ignatius Loyola - Founder of the Jesuits; spearhead of the Counter Reformation.
James Watt - Improved the steam engine (1769) - the Industrial Revolution's heart.
Karl Marx - Philosopher of scientific socialism: Communist Manifesto (1848) with Engels; Das Kapital (1867).
Robert Owen - Factory reformer and utopian socialist; New Lanark experiment.

blocks.text: Renaissance vs Reformation: Cultural-intellectual rebirth of art and learning versus religious reform splitting the Church.
Reformation vs Counter Reformation: Protestant breakaway from Rome versus the Catholic Church's internal reform and response.
Capitalism vs Socialism: Private ownership for profit versus social/state ownership for equal benefit.
Renaissance art vs Medieval art: Realism, perspective, human subjects versus flat, symbolic, church-dominated imagery.

items: Saying the Renaissance began in Germany - it began in Italy.
Reversing the dates of the printing press (c. 1440-50) and Constantinople's fall (1453).
Writing that Luther's theses started as a call for a new church - he first sought reform within; excommunication came later.
Calling the Counter Reformation purely repressive - it included genuine reform (Council of Trent) and education (Jesuits).
Starting the Industrial Revolution in 1850 - it spans roughly 1750-1850, beginning in Britain.
Confusing socialism (social ownership) with communism as identical without nuance - Marx's communism is socialism's radical stage.

questions.prompt: State any two causes of the Renaissance.
questions.answer: Any two of: the capture of Constantinople (1453) driving Greek scholars and manuscripts to Italy; the decline of feudalism freeing towns and minds; new trade routes and the wealth of Italian city-states; the spirit of enquiry fostered by discoveries; Gutenberg's printing press spreading books.

questions.prompt: What were the causes of the Reformation?
questions.answer: Dissatisfaction with the practices of the Catholic Church - sale of indulgences, simony, nepotism, clerical immorality and the cost of St Peter's; the new learning of the Renaissance, which led men to read the Bible (Erasmus's Greek New Testament) and judge for themselves; rulers' resentment of papal interference and taxes; the printing press spreading criticism.
questions.explanation: Church abuses + new learning + political + press.

questions.prompt: Define capitalism and state any two causes for its rise.
questions.answer: Capitalism is an economic system in which private persons own the means of production and produce for profit in a competitive market, hiring wage labour. Causes of its rise: profits of colonial trade and banking; the price revolution rewarding enterprise; enclosures creating free labour; inventions making factory investment profitable; laissez-faire policies protecting property and contracts.

questions.prompt: How did the Industrial Revolution give rise to socialism?
questions.answer: Factories concentrated workers in cities with long hours, low wages, child and female labour, and slum housing; wealth pooled among factory owners while labour stayed poor; trade cycles threw thousands out of work. Reformers answered first with factory acts, unions and model villages (Owen's New Lanark); radical thinkers (Marx and Engels, Communist Manifesto 1848) taught that exploitation was built into capitalism and called for social ownership of the means of production. Thus the miseries and inequalities of industrial capitalism directly produced socialism.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between the Reformation and the Counter Reformation.
questions.answer: The Reformation was the protest movement that broke with Rome: Luther (1517), Calvin, Zwingli and Henry VIII founded reformed churches teaching scripture's authority, faith and vernacular worship. The Counter Reformation was the Catholic Church's answer: the Council of Trent (1545-63) corrected abuses and reaffirmed doctrine, the Jesuits (Loyola) led education and missions, and the Inquisition repressed heresy - recovering much of southern Europe. One split the Church; the other reformed and re-armed it.
questions.explanation: Direction (break vs response), agents and results.
questions.commonMistake: Calling the Counter Reformation part of the Reformation.

questions.prompt: Describe the causes of the Industrial Revolution and assess its social consequences.
questions.answer: Causes: (1) capital accumulated from colonial and maritime trade, with raw materials (cotton) and markets supplied by colonies; (2) Britain's coal and iron, linked by canals and roads; (3) the agricultural revolution - enclosures and crop rotation - which raised food output and freed rural labour for factories; (4) a chain of inventions: Kay's flying shuttle (1733), Hargreaves's spinning jenny (1764), Arkwright's water frame, Crompton's mule, Cartwright's power loom, and above all Watt's steam engine (1769); (5) political stability, patent protection and laissez-faire policy encouraging enterprise. Social consequences: the factory system and urbanisation created crowded industrial cities with slums; long hours, low wages and child labour marked early factory life; a propertyless working class emerged beside a new industrial middle class; trade unions, factory acts and reform movements followed; and the inequality of the system generated socialism (Owen to Marx), reshaping politics for the next century.
questions.explanation: Five causes + social consequences with examples.

questions.prompt: Arrange in chronological order: Fall of Constantinople, Communist Manifesto, Luther's Theses, Watt's steam engine.
questions.answer: Fall of Constantinople (1453) -> Luther's Ninety-Five Theses (1517) -> Watt's steam engine (1769) -> Communist Manifesto (1848).
questions.commonMistake: Placing the steam engine before the Theses.
